extracted.intended_audience: students and educated readers of natural philosophy / evolutionary theory
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook/chapter exposition of the 'law of evolution' emphasizing two complementary processes — progressive integration and progressive differentiation (compound evolution) — with cross-domain illustrations (astronomic, geological, biological, social).

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Alike during the evolution of the Solar System, of a planet, of an organism, of a nation, there is progressive aggregation of the entire mass; increasing density and drawing in of previously separate matter; loss of relative motion; and increasing co-ordination and mutual dependence among parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: concentration of a nebula into sun, planets, satellites; growth of organs in organisms; rise of special industrial centres and mutually-dependent divisions of Science. Integration implies both local consolidation of parts and increased combinative closeness among parts producing cooperative assemblages; the more developed the system the more its parts are mutually dependent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound evolution (progressive differentiation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where secondary re-distributions of matter and motion accompany primary integration, complexity and heterogeneity arise — the components of a mass while becoming integrated also become differentiated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The distinction between simple evolution (integration without secondary re-distributions) and compound evolution (integration accompanied by secondary re-distributions) — compound evolution is identified with the transformation from homogeneity to multiformity. This is the central theme of the chapter and the universal expression sought for structural modifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary re-distributions produce structural modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary re-distributions that occur in aggregates of medium coherence produce relatively persistent structural modifications (rather than merely evanescent results).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In very incoherent aggregates secondary effects are transient; but in aggregates that attain and maintain a medium state, secondary re-distributions create lasting structures. The inquiry centers on finding a universal expression for these structural modifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heterogeneity in astronomical systems as indicator of differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Growing variety of structure throughout the sidereal system (nebulas of different forms, star groups from scattered to dense clusters, contrasts of size, colour, spectra) implies progressive differentiation accompanying aggregation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Solar System's concentration produced marked heterogeneities (sun vs planets in bulk, light, temperature; planet-to-planet contrasts in heat received, inclinations, specific gravities, physical constitution). These celestial examples illustrate secondary re-distributions that accompany primary concentration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geological differentiation and climatic heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: The Earth's cooling and solidification, repeated deposition of strata, igneous action and crustal movements have progressively increased heterogeneity of the Earth's structure, surface, and climates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: multiplication and increasing complexity of strata; tilting, faults, metallic veins; growth of mountain systems; changes in land/sea distribution producing local climatic distinctions. These processes produce that every extensive region and locality tends to have its own meteorologic and structural conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ontogenetic progression from homogeneity to heterogeneity (Von Baer's law applied broadly)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every plant and animal during individual development passes from an initially homogeneous state (germ/ovum as chemically and structurally uniform) to an increasingly heterogeneous one (chemical segregation, tissue differentiation, organ formation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chemical differentiation: segregation of nitrogenous and non-nitrogenous compounds, local formation of chlorophyll vs cellulose, starch to sugar to gum, formation of wood and cork. Structural differentiation: cells diverge into tissues (e.g., chlorophyll-cells, spongy mesophyll), formation of vessels, cartilage to bone, formation of organs from initially similar buds. The ontogenetic process is viewed as a microcosm of compound evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting the fossil/phylogenetic record cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: Fossil evidence for increasing heterogeneity through geological time is fragmentary and open to dispute; negative evidence is weak and the record is influenced by accessibility, preservation, metamorphism, and geological transformations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveats and counter-arguments: two-thirds of Earth's surface is underwater; many regions are unexplored; earlier strata may have been destroyed by igneous action; repeated discoveries (vertebrates where none were thought to exist) show limits of negative inference. Uniformitarian and progressionist readings each have plausible replies; breaks in succession can be explained by geological subsidences and elevations. Despite limitations, some palaeontologic facts (incremental community of type between adjacent strata, intermediate forms like Palaeotherium) are consistent with evolution from less to more heterogeneous forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human biological and social differentiation as exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: Man, both as an individual organism and as socially embodied, shows pronounced advance from homogeneity to heterogeneity: biological (limb proportions, cranial vs facial bone ratios, cerebral development) and social (division of labour, hereditary rule, occupational specialization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: civilized Europeans show greater limb and cranial differentiation than so-called 'lower' races; infants retain primitive resemblances that diverge in development; social evolution shows early homogeneity of roles in tribes, later differentiation of governing vs governed, hereditary rulers who cease to provide for their own wants, and increasing occupational specialization as society advances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity and geometrical progression of differentiations
rubrics_metrics.description: A first difference between parts leads to further differences within those parts, and so on, producing a multiplication of differences (often likened to geometric progression) until the complex adult/whole is formed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied across domains: tissues subdivide into sub-tissues, organs diversify from similar buds, social roles multiply from initial slight distinctions. The process underlies formation of classes, subclasses, organs, and social institutions; it is the chief mechanism by which compound evolution yields complex wholes.
